---
title: "The method"
---

System identification here is an iterative, information-optimal loop built on the
**Pintelon–Schoukens frequency-domain method**. Two facts drive the design:
**measurement time on a real interferometer is expensive**, and **drive amplitude
is bounded by actuator saturation** — so both must be spent wisely. Rather than
sweeping uniformly across frequency and hoping for the best, `system_ident` solves
the inverse problem: *given a prior model and a fixed drive-power budget, where
should the excitation energy go to extract the most information about the model
parameters?* — then measures **leakage-free** and fits by **maximum likelihood**.

The answer to *where* comes from Fisher information theory; the answer to *how to
measure and fit* comes from the periodic-multisine, leakage-free FRF and the
Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimator.

## The loop

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-loop
%%| fig-cap: "The Pintelon–Schoukens identification loop. Each pass redesigns the excitation from the improved model; the loop stops when the Cramér–Rao fractional uncertainty drops below target."
flowchart LR
  A(["Prior model<br/>+ error bars"]):::start --> B["<b>Design</b><br/>optimal multisine<br/>dispersion ν(f)"]:::design
  B --> C["<b>Inject + read</b><br/>Schroeder phases<br/>Tukey-ramped"]:::act
  C --> D["<b>Measure</b><br/>leakage-free reference FRF<br/>synchronous DFT, per-bin σ"]:::act
  D --> E["<b>Accumulate</b><br/>inverse-variance<br/>across passes"]:::act
  E --> F["<b>Fit</b><br/>ML (GMLEstimator)<br/>Gauss-Newton / LM"]:::fit
  F --> G{"<b>Fisher / CRB</b><br/>σ/θ &lt; target?"}:::test
  G -- "no — redesign from<br/>the improved model" --> B
  G -- yes --> H(["Done<br/>parameters at the CRB"]):::done
```

::: {.column-margin}
**Pass 1 is special.** It uses a *prior-robust* drive spread over $f_0(1\pm u)$, so even a
far (±50 %) prior still puts power where the true resonance is; later passes concentrate
once the model is trusted.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## One sentence

Given a prior model, `system_ident` computes exactly how much each frequency
contributes to parameter information, lays a periodic multisine there, measures
its frequency response *without spectral leakage*, fits the plant by maximum
likelihood, and repeats — converging to parameter uncertainties at the
Cramér–Rao bound, far below what equal-power flat excitation can achieve.
:::

Each iteration does five things:

1. **Design** — compute the dispersion function $\nu(f)$ from the current model,
   the quiet-time readout-noise PSD $P_{yy}(f)$, and the drive budget; run the
   Pintelon–Schoukens fixed-point iteration to obtain the optimal excitation PSD
   $P_{xx}(f)$. (See [Fisher & excitation](fisher.qmd).)

2. **Inject** — realise $P_{xx}(f)$ as a **periodic multisine**: a sum of
   harmonically related sinusoids whose period is exactly the analysis window,
   tiled over the record and Tukey-ramped at the leading edge. The phases are
   the deterministic **Schroeder phases**, which minimise the crest factor so a
   saturation-limited actuator carries the most in-band power for a fixed peak.
   Inject through the backend (twin or CDS hardware) and read both the drive
   monitor and the response.

3. **Measure (leakage-free)** — because the drive is periodic over the window, a
   synchronous (integer-period) DFT of the response is **leakage-free**. The FRF
   is the *reference-based, ratio-of-averages* estimate
   $\hat H = \overline{Y}/\overline{X}$ (period-averaged spectra), and the per-bin
   noise covariance comes from the **period-to-period scatter** of the residual.
   Leading periods that still carry the start transient are dropped.

4. **Accumulate** — inverse-variance-weight the new FRF estimate with all previous
   ones, frequency bin by frequency bin. The first pass uses a *prior-robust*
   excitation spread over the plausible resonance band; the accumulated estimate
   carries that band coverage forward permanently while later concentrated passes
   sharpen the resonances.

5. **Fit (maximum likelihood)** — re-fit the model on the accumulated FRF with the
   `GMLEstimator`, minimising the Gaussian negative-log-likelihood by
   Gauss-Newton / Levenberg–Marquardt. Update the Fisher information, read off the
   Cramér–Rao parameter covariance, and test the fractional-uncertainty stop
   criterion.

## Why a periodic multisine?

A one-off random record is *not* periodic over the analysis window, so its DFT
**leaks**: a sharp resonance smears its power into neighbouring bins, biasing the
near-peak measurement exactly where the information is densest. Windowing reduces
the leakage but distorts the bin shape and throws away record. A **periodic
multisine** sidesteps the problem entirely — over an integer number of periods the
synchronous DFT is leakage-free by construction, so a high-$Q$ mode is measured at
its true peak with no near-resonance bias (Pintelon & Schoukens, *System
Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach*, 2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press, 2012 —
periodic excitation and leakage-free measurement). Tiling many periods also gives
an *internal*, model-free noise estimate: the scatter of the per-period response
about its average is the measurement uncertainty on each bin, with no assumption
about the noise shape.

The **Schroeder phases** (P&S §4) set the relative phase of each line so the
waveform's peak-to-RMS ratio (crest factor) is near-minimal. Under a hard actuator
limit this is what lets the drive deliver substantial in-band power without
clipping — a random-phase multisine of the same RMS would saturate far sooner.

## Why a reference-based FRF?

The estimate is the *ratio of period-averaged spectra*
$\hat H = \overline{Y}/\overline{X}$, **not** the average of per-period ratios and
**not** the cross-/auto-spectrum estimator $S_{yx}/S_{xx}$. Averaging the complex
spectra projects the response onto the *known, deterministic* multisine, which is
uncorrelated with the loop and sensor noise. In **closed loop** this is decisive:
the controller feeds sensor noise back onto the drive, so $S_{yx}/S_{xx}$ is biased,
but the reference-based ratio cancels the controller and returns the *open-loop
plant* — with no controller model and no division by a fed-back signal (the
Pintelon–Schoukens closed-loop / reference-based measurement). Because the drive
monitor itself supplies $X$, no separate reference channel is needed.

## Why maximum likelihood?

Once the FRF and its per-bin noise covariance are in hand, the **Gaussian
maximum-likelihood** estimator is the right way to turn them into model
parameters. Minimising

$$
\mathcal{C}(\theta) \;=\; \sum_k
  \frac{\bigl|\,\hat H(f_k) - G(f_k;\theta)\,\bigr|^2}{\sigma^2(f_k)}
$$

(the $\sigma(f_k)$ are the measured per-bin standard errors) is the
Pintelon–Schoukens Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimator: **asymptotically
unbiased** and **efficient** — it attains the Cramér–Rao bound when the noise
weights are correct. Weighting each residual by its own measured variance is what
makes the
fit trust the well-measured resonance bins and discount the noisy ones, instead of
the uniform weighting an unweighted least-squares fit would impose.

## Why Fisher information?

The Fisher information matrix $I(\theta)$ bounds how precisely *any* unbiased
estimator can recover parameters $\theta$ from data; its inverse $I(\theta)^{-1}$
is the Cramér–Rao lower bound on the parameter covariance. For an LTI system driven
by a stationary input with PSD $P_{xx}(f)$ and measured in readout noise with PSD
$P_{yy}(f)$ over time $T$:

$$
I_{ij}(\theta) = 2\,T \int
  \frac{P_{xx}(f)}{P_{yy}(f)} \,
  \operatorname{Re}\!\left[
    \frac{\partial G^*(f;\theta)}{\partial \theta_i}
    \frac{\partial G(f;\theta)}{\partial \theta_j}
  \right] df .
$$

The optimal $P_{xx}(f)$ maximises $\log\det I(\theta)$ — the log-volume of the
information ellipsoid, the **D-optimal** design criterion — subject to
$\int P_{xx}(f)\,df = \text{const}$ (fixed power budget). Its fixed point is the
**dispersion-function** reweighting implemented in `design.pintelon`
(P&S §5.4.2); see [Fisher & excitation](fisher.qmd) for the construction.

## Why iterative?

The optimal excitation depends on the current model through the Jacobian
$\partial G/\partial\theta$ and hence through the dispersion function. As the model
improves pass by pass, so does the excitation design — the loop progressively
sharpens its focus toward the frequencies that are most informative *given what it
has already learned*.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The first pass is special

`SysIDLoop` runs pass 1 with a **prior-robust** excitation: the optimal drive
averaged over the prior's plausible resonance band $f_0(1\pm u)$, so even a far
(±50 %) prior still puts power where the true resonance is. This samples the
transfer function broadly before later passes concentrate on the located
features — keeping the maximum-likelihood refit well conditioned and avoiding a
local minimum from poor initial coverage.
:::

## References

Pintelon & Schoukens, *System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach*,
2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press, 2012 — periodic / leakage-free measurement and the
reference-based (closed-loop) FRF; multisine design and Schroeder phases (§4);
dispersion-function optimal input design (§5.4.2); and the Gaussian
maximum-likelihood estimator with its Cramér–Rao efficiency.

[LIGO-G2101503](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G2101503) — Fisher-information
expressions for suspension parameters (the form carried by `fisher.fisher_matrix`).

[LIGO-G1400084](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G1400084) (Larry Price) — original
motivation and prior work.
